extracted.intended_audience: conference program chairs, area chairs, reviewers, and researchers interested in peer-review reliability/consistency
extracted.subtask_description: Measuring and analyzing decision consistency in conference peer review by duplicating a random subset of submissions, assigning independent committees, and comparing outcomes and reviewer/AC behavior. Includes procedural implementation, outcome metrics, and analysis of limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation of duplication (10% random duplicated papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the assignment phase we chose 10% of papers uniformly at random — 'duplicated papers.' We assigned two Area Chairs (ACs) and twice the normal number of reviewers to these papers. We created a copy of each paper and split the ACs and reviewers at random between the two copies. We made sure the two ACs were assigned to two different Senior Area Chairs (SACs) so that no SAC handled both copies of the same paper. Any newly invited reviewer for one copy was automatically added as a conflict for the other copy. The papers' committees were not told about the experiment and were not aware the paper had been duplicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural constraints to avoid information leakage between committees: random selection of 10% of submissions; duplicate record creation; split ACs/reviewers randomly; ensure SAC separation; add reciprocal conflicts for newly invited reviewers; keep committees unaware. Authors notified only right before initial reviews released and asked to respond independently and keep confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rule for duplicated papers
rubrics_metrics.description: As in 2014, duplicated papers were accepted if at least one of the two copies was recommended for acceptance and no 'fatal flaw' was found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes how to decide final outcome when duplicate committees disagree. Examples: 92 accepted papers that would not have been accepted without the experiment; if one committee finds a fatal flaw, that can override the other committee's acceptance. In cases where committees disagreed about whether a flaw was 'fatal', conditional acceptance with jointly determined conditions was used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraction of inconsistent outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The fraction of duplicated papers that were accepted by only one of the two committees (as either a poster, a spotlight, or an oral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported value: 203 out of 882 = 23.0%. This is a primary metric for measuring decision inconsistency between independent committees reviewing the same submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-baseline comparison for inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare observed inconsistency to the expected fraction if acceptance decisions were made at random with the observed acceptance probability (random baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with an average acceptance rate of 22.7%, the random baseline predicts 35.1% inconsistent outcomes. Observed 23.0% is closer to random than to zero; express improvements relative to this baseline (e.g., 35% relative improvement in 2014). Visualized as a gray curve mapping acceptance probability to expected inconsistent fraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusted inconsistency excluding 'bumpable' labels
rubrics_metrics.description: If we don't consider 'Accept that can be bumped down' vs 'Reject', and 'Reject that can be bumped up' vs 'Poster Accept that shouldn't be bumped up to Spotlight' as inconsistent, the fraction of inconsistent outcomes drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this narrower definition reduces observed inconsistency from 23.0% to 16.0%. This shows how label semantics ('can be bumped up/down') affect measured disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept precision / arbitrariness (probability accepted->rejected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraction of papers accepted by one committee that were rejected by the other (also framed as 'complement to 1 of accept precision' or 'arbitrariness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported value: 50.6% in 2021 (compared to 49.5% in 2014). Also reported: probability a randomly chosen rejected paper would have been accepted upon re-review: 14.9% in 2021 (17.5% in 2014). This measures stability of positive/negative decisions under re-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disagreement intensity on high-status selections (orals/spotlights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of how often committees disagree specifically about selecting papers for orals and spotlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: especially high disagreement for orals and spotlights — more than half of all spotlights recommended by either committee were rejected by the other (examples: 13/25 and 13/23). If accepting only orals/spotlights, the committees agreed on very few papers (3 agreed out of 29 and 25 recommended), illustrating higher arbitrariness when selection is more selective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of shifting acceptance threshold on inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how the fraction of inconsistent outcomes changes if the acceptance threshold is moved (e.g., accept only orals/spotlights, bump down posters, bump up rejects marked 'bumpable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: accepting only orals/spotlights gives only a small improvement over random baseline (3% relative improvement); bumping down posters marked as candidates for being bumped down yields a 25% relative improvement; decisions by ACs and bumping up reject-candidates yield a 35% relative improvement. Use the gray random-baseline curve to visualize the impact across acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal behavior after initial reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Include withdrawn papers in analysis and measure withdrawal rates after initial reviews; compare rates between duplicated and non-duplicated papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 118 papers were withdrawn after initial reviews and were included. Authors were most likely to withdraw if both copies were headed for rejection. Withdrawal rate after seeing initial reviews was 45% higher for papers not in the experiment compared with duplicated papers, possibly because duplicated papers had two shots at acceptance. This behavior affects observed acceptance rates and is a confounder for consistency measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: AC/SAC feedback categories explaining disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: From feedback on disagreement cases, three main categories explain why committees disagreed: (1) 'noise on the decision frontier' (borderline papers), (2) genuine disagreements about contribution value or severity of limitations, and (3) cases where one committee found a significant issue the other did not (e.g., close prior work, incorrect proofs, methodological flaws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey responses: 48% labeled as borderline/no real disagreement; 45% 'I still stand by our committee's decision'; 7% 'I believe the other committee made the right decision.' Limited sample (feedback on 99 of 203 disputed papers, and both committees responded for only 18) constrains conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' response-behavior confound
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of duplicated papers were asked to respond to each set of reviews independently, but some authors put more effort into the copy they thought more likely to be accepted; some authors only left comments on the copy with the higher average score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed: 50 pairs where authors only left comments on the higher-scoring copy. Acceptance rate differences between duplicated and non-duplicated papers (22.7% vs 25.8%) have non-overlapping 95% binomial CIs, suggesting authors changing behavior may account for some differences and thus confound the experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration edits and metadata inconsistencies as a data quality limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When decisions shifted as part of calibration, ACs were often asked to edit their meta-reviews to move a paper between classes without updating the 'can be bumped up/down' fields, producing nonsensical combinations (e.g., 'reject' and 'can be bumped down').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inconsistencies can introduce minor inaccuracies into analysis that uses those labels to determine inconsistency; authors observed nine such cases and warn about potential small impacts on shifted-threshold analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to past experiment (2014) as historical benchmark
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextualize 2021 results against the 2014 NeurIPS experiment: in 2014, 25.9% disagreement on duplicated papers (166 duplicated), with a 25% acceptance rate and a random baseline of 37.5% disagreement (31% relative improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical results to assess whether noise has changed with scale; the blog concludes results are consistent with 2014 despite large growth in submissions, suggesting no evidence decision process noise changed with scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative guidance for program chairs (selectivity vs arbitrariness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical takeaway: being significantly more selective appears to increase arbitrariness (fraction of accepted papers that would differ upon rereview); increasing acceptance rate may not appreciably decrease arbitrariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a numerical metric but policy guidance based on the observed relationship between selectivity and inconsistency; chairs should consider trade-offs between selectivity and decision stability. Also: encourage authors not to be excessively discouraged by rejections because the review process can be noisier than the paper's absolute quality.
